case_info.scenario: A 32-year-old female patient presented with chronic discharging sinus with recurrent infection at the left sternoclavicular joint (SCJ). A skin dimple with a little mucouslike secretion had been noticed since birth. Local painful swelling and abscess formation of the cutaneous pit began at age 4 years and subsided after intravenous antibiotics and incision. Thereafter, 5 similar infection episodes occurred in the last 20 years. There was no family history of similar disorders. Physical examination showed a 2.8 × 2.5-cm, reddish, elevated scarlike plaque with a 6-mm sinus orifice containing mucouslike exudate at the left SCJ (Figure 1A). Magnetic resonance imaging revealed a 23 × 14-mm irregular subcutaneous tract with low T1-weighted and high T2-weighted signal intensity extending toward the left SCJ (Figure 1B). The distance between the tract bottom and sternal end of the left clavicle was approximately 1.5 mm. Intraoperative laryngoscopy found no pyriform fistula. The sinus with adjacent scar tissue was completely excised under general anesthesia after sinus staining with methylene blue. The sinus terminated at the fascia of the clavicular head of the left sternocleidomastoid muscle. Postoperative histopathology uncovered that the sinus was lined by keratinizing squamous epithelium with pilosebaceous glands and intraluminal keratinous materials.

B, Sagittal T2-weighted, fat-suppressed magnetic resonance image (MRI) showed an irregular hyperintense tract (arrowhead) extending toward the left sternoclavicular joint (circle).
case_info.explanation: Sternoclavicular sinus (SCS), or sinus sternoclavicularis, is a relatively uncommon congenital sinus near the SCJ.1It is also named as congenital sternoclavicular dermoid sinus and congenital dermoid fistula/sinus of the anterior chest region due to its similar characteristics of dermoid cysts.1,2To date, approximately 389 cases have been reported, of which 56.6% are females and 85.3% are left sided.3-5Its embryological origin is still debatable. First, SCS may be analogue to dermoid cysts resulting from entrapment of epithelial elements in the deeper tissues along embryonic fusion lines.1Second, SCS could originate from a disorderly fusion between the upper sternum and proximal clavicle.3However, both would explain the blind ending near the SCJ but does not account for the left-sided predominance and occasionally endodermal origin of ciliated epithelium and salivary glands.1,6Third, considering that its sinus occurring predominantly in the left side and locating at the sternoclavicular end of the sternocleidomastoid muscle correspond to the anatomical position of the fourth branchial cleft, some authors propose that SCS may represent the cutaneous remnant of fourth branchial cleft.1,3,4,7 SCS typically manifests as a cutaneous pit, sinus, or infected mass near the SCJ with a left-sided predominance. Despite its presentation at birth, it often becomes apparent only after infection.2,4Recurrent infections and abscesses are common, while the pyriform sinus and thyroid gland are unaffected. The sinus tract is relatively short and ends blindly at the deep surface of the platysma muscle or the superficial surface of the clavicular head of the sternocleidomastoid muscle.3,4Histopathologically, the sinus tract is predominantly lined with squamous epithelium with adnexal structures including pilosebaceous and sweat glands, and occasionally with ciliated epithelium (Figure 2).4,6 Clinical diagnosis of SCS is usually straightforward based on medical history and clinical presentations. A skin streak sign, a pale skin streak extending superiorly from the sinus orifice toward the ipsilateral thyroid gland, may be diagnostic.4Imaging examinations are useful for identifying the sinus tract’s length and path. Ultrasonography is preferable for initial evaluation, whereas computed tomography and magnetic resonance imaging are helpful to demystify the extent of SCS, especially if there are other anatomical anomalies.4-6 Main differential diagnoses comprise epidermoid cysts, dermoid cysts, and branchial cleft anomalies.2,4Epidermoid and dermoid cysts develop from entrapment of epithelial structures during closure of the branchial arches and often locate along the midline,8and their cystic walls are lined by keratinized squamous epithelium with or without adnexal structures in dermoid or epidermoid cysts, respectively.2,4Branchial cleft anomalies result from a failure to obliterate the embryonic branchial apparatus, and their cyst/sinus walls are composed of either squamous or ciliated epithelium. Second branchial sinus/fistula is the most common subtype, with its external orifice locating above the SCJ and along the anterior border of the sternocleidomastoid muscle, and its course running in a cranial direction. Third and fourth branchial anomalies often possess an internal opening in the lateral wall of the pyriform sinus, and present with recurrent neck abscess and acute suppurative thyroiditis.2,4,9 Because of the risk of infection and abscess formation, complete resection of the sinus tract from skin orifice to the blind end during quiescent inflammation phase is recommended.1-5Intrasinus cannulation and methylene blue stain can facilitate en bloc resection of sinus tract.5,9This patient underwent complete excision of the entire sinus tract with surrounding scar tissue using methylene blue stain, with no complications and relapse at 2-month follow-up.

* Use the full 1-5 range. 5 marks the most demanding message you would realistically
  encounter in THIS conversation, not a once-in-a-career extreme -- do not collapse a
  genuinely very-high-workload turn down to 4 just because something even more extreme is

[NASA-TLX-derived scoring dimensions]

1. Mental Demand
   Definition: 
   - how much mental and perceptual activity is required, such as thinking, deciding, calculating, remembering, looking, or searching.
   - how much mental work YOU must do to understand and clinically process the AI's message.

   Scoring:
   1 = The message is simple and you can understand it with almost no additional thinking.
       Example: "I agree. The findings you mentioned support your current diagnosis."
   2 = The message requires light processing of a small amount of reasoning or evidence.
       Example: "That seems reasonable. Could you confirm whether the fever began before
       or after the rash?"
   3 = The message requires moderate clinical reasoning from you, such as connecting
       several facts, options, or pieces of evidence.
       Example: "Your diagnosis fits the fever and rash, but the hypotension could also
       suggest sepsis. Can we compare those possibilities briefly?"
   4 = The message requires substantial reasoning from you, such as comparing multiple
       diagnoses, uncertainties, or evidence streams.
       Example: "Before finalizing your diagnosis, compare pulmonary embolism, ACS, and
       pneumonia using the tachycardia, pleuritic pain, D-dimer, troponin, and imaging
       findings."
   5 = The message requires very complex reasoning from you, such as deeply revising your
       differential or holding several competing diagnoses against multiple evidence streams
       at once. This does NOT require a literal "from scratch" rebuild -- being asked to
       compare three or more diagnoses across several findings AND explain how each fits or
       is ruled out already qualifies.
       Example: "Your current diagnosis may not explain the key findings. Compare PE, ACS,
       pneumonia, and aortic dissection: for each, state which evidence supports or rules
       it out, and explain which best fits the overall picture."

2. Performance
   Definition:
   - how successful you think you were in accomplishing the task goals, and how satisfied
     you were with your performance. Performance is anchored from Good to Poor.
   - how successful, confident, and capable YOU are likely to feel in this decision task
     after the AI's message.
   - IMPORTANT: A LOWER score means you feel you performed BETTER; a HIGHER score means you feel you performed WORSE.

   Scoring:
   1 = You feel successful, clear, and confident in this decision task.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is consistent with the key findings, especially X and Y."
   2 = You feel mostly successful, with only minor uncertainty.
       Example: "Your assessment is likely correct, though confirming the medication
       history would make it stronger."
   3 = You feel moderately uncertain or in need of additional checking.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is plausible, but one finding does not fully fit. We
       should check whether another diagnosis explains it better."
   4 = You feel your judgment is weak, incomplete, or possibly wrong.
       Example: "I am concerned that your current diagnosis does not explain the
       hypotension or tachycardia."
   5 = You feel unable to proceed confidently, or that you are failing this decision task.
       Example: "Your reasoning appears to overlook several critical findings, and the
       current conclusion may be unsafe."
   This is NEVER about whether you are objectively right. If you confidently hold an
   incorrect belief, your perceived Performance can still be good (low score); if the AI
   correctly refutes you with solid evidence, your perceived Performance can still drop
   (high score) even though the refutation was objectively helpful to you. Rate only how
   successful and in-control YOU feel, never accuracy.

3. Effort
   Definition:
   - how hard you had to work mentally and physically to accomplish your level of
     performance.
   - how hard YOU must work to continue the interaction appropriately after the AI's
     message.

   Scoring:
   1 = Almost no effort; you can passively read, accept, or acknowledge.
       Example: "Agreed. Your choice is consistent with the case."
   2 = Low effort; a short confirmation or simple recall is enough.
       Example: "Can you confirm whether the patient had recent travel?"
   3 = Moderate effort; you must explain, organize, or provide some reasoning.
       Example: "Can you briefly explain why you think pneumonia is more likely than PE?"
   4 = High effort; you must compare evidence, revise your reasoning, or justify a choice.
       Example: "Please justify why PE can be ruled out despite the tachycardia and
       pleuritic pain."
   5 = Very high effort; you must defend your judgment on multiple fronts at once, or rule
       out several alternatives with explicit evidence. This does NOT require a literal
       "rebuild from scratch" -- being pushed to justify your stance against three or more
       competing options already qualifies.
       Example: "For each of PE, ACS, and pneumonia, explain which evidence supports or
       rules it out, and defend why you still prefer your current diagnosis."
   Do not confuse this with Mental Demand: "Compare PE, ACS, and pneumonia using the
   evidence" has high Mental Demand (a lot to think through) but if no reply is required of
   you, Effort can stay low -- you only have to read and absorb it. Conversely, "You said PE
   is unlikely. Please justify that." is short and easy to understand (Mental Demand may be
   only moderate) but forces you to actively construct a defense, so Effort is high. Effort
   is about how much active work YOU must produce, not how complex the input was.

4. Frustration
   Definition:
   - how insecure, discouraged, irritated, stressed, or annoyed you felt, as opposed to
     secure, gratified, content, relaxed, or complacent.
   - how much irritation, stress, pressure, discouragement, or loss of autonomy the AI's
     message imposes on YOU.

   Scoring:
   1 = Very low frustration; the message is calm, respectful, and unlikely to pressure you.
       Example: "That reasoning makes sense. One small point to keep in mind is X."
   2 = Low frustration; mild discomfort is possible but it remains easy for you to continue.
       Example: "I may be missing something, but could we double-check whether X fits
       the case?"
   3 = Moderate frustration; the AI raises concerns, disagreement, or uncertainty in a
       somewhat pressuring way.
       Example: "I am concerned that this diagnosis may not explain the tachycardia.
       Could you justify why you still prefer it?"
   4 = High frustration; the AI strongly challenges you or may trigger your defensiveness.
       Example: "This seems like a serious oversight. You need to explain why you are
       dismissing PE."
   5 = Very high frustration; you may feel undermined, dismissed, attacked, or pressured.
       Example: "Your reasoning is clearly flawed, and proceeding with your diagnosis
       would be unsafe."
   Frustration is not just "the AI disagreed with me" -- it is about HOW the disagreement is
   delivered. A polite challenge ("One concern is that the current diagnosis may not fully
   explain the tachycardia. Could we check PE before finalizing?") should score low-to-mid
   even though it is a real challenge. An aggressive or repetitive one ("You still haven't
   justified why PE is ruled out. This is a serious oversight.") should score high.

A skin dimple with a little mucouslike secretion had been noticed since birth. case_info.explanation: Sternoclavicular sinus (SCS), or sinus sternoclavicularis, is a relatively uncommon congenital sinus near the SCJ.1It is also named as congenital sternoclavicular dermoid sinus and congenital dermoid fistula/sinus of the anterior chest region due to its similar characteristics of dermoid cysts.1,2To date, approximately 389 cases have been reported, of which 56.6% are females and 85.3% are left sided.3-5Its embryological origin is still debatable. First, SCS may be analogue to dermoid cysts resulting from entrapment of epithelial elements in the deeper tissues along embryonic fusion lines.1Second, SCS could originate from a disorderly fusion between the upper sternum and proximal clavicle.3However, both would explain the blind ending near the SCJ but does not account for the left-sided predominance and occasionally endodermal origin of ciliated epithelium and salivary glands.1,6Third, considering that its sinus occurring predominantly in the left side and locating at the sternoclavicular end of the sternocleidomastoid muscle correspond to the anatomical position of the fourth branchial cleft, some authors propose that SCS may represent the cutaneous remnant of fourth branchial cleft.1,3,4,7 SCS typically manifests as a cutaneous pit, sinus, or infected mass near the SCJ with a left-sided predominance. Despite its presentation at birth, it often becomes apparent only after infection.2,4Recurrent infections and abscesses are common, while the pyriform sinus and thyroid gland are unaffected. The sinus tract is relatively short and ends blindly at the deep surface of the platysma muscle or the superficial surface of the clavicular head of the sternocleidomastoid muscle.3,4Histopathologically, the sinus tract is predominantly lined with squamous epithelium with adnexal structures including pilosebaceous and sweat glands, and occasionally with ciliated epithelium (Figure 2).4,6 Clinical diagnosis of SCS is usually straightforward based on medical history and clinical presentations. A skin streak sign, a pale skin streak extending superiorly from the sinus orifice toward the ipsilateral thyroid gland, may be diagnostic.4Imaging examinations are useful for identifying the sinus tract’s length and path. Ultrasonography is preferable for initial evaluation, whereas computed tomography and magnetic resonance imaging are helpful to demystify the extent of SCS, especially if there are other anatomical anomalies.4-6 Main differential diagnoses comprise epidermoid cysts, dermoid cysts, and branchial cleft anomalies.2,4Epidermoid and dermoid cysts develop from entrapment of epithelial structures during closure of the branchial arches and often locate along the midline,8and their cystic walls are lined by keratinized squamous epithelium with or without adnexal structures in dermoid or epidermoid cysts, respectively.2,4Branchial cleft anomalies result from a failure to obliterate the embryonic branchial apparatus, and their cyst/sinus walls are composed of either squamous or ciliated epithelium. Second branchial sinus/fistula is the most common subtype, with its external orifice locating above the SCJ and along the anterior border of the sternocleidomastoid muscle, and its course running in a cranial direction. Third and fourth branchial anomalies often possess an internal opening in the lateral wall of the pyriform sinus, and present with recurrent neck abscess and acute suppurative thyroiditis.2,4,9 Because of the risk of infection and abscess formation, complete resection of the sinus tract from skin orifice to the blind end during quiescent inflammation phase is recommended.1-5Intrasinus cannulation and methylene blue stain can facilitate en bloc resection of sinus tract.5,9This patient underwent complete excision of the entire sinus tract with surrounding scar tissue using methylene blue stain, with no complications and relapse at 2-month follow-up.

case_info.explanation: Sternoclavicular sinus (SCS), or sinus sternoclavicularis, is a relatively uncommon congenital sinus near the SCJ.1It is also named as congenital sternoclavicular dermoid sinus and congenital dermoid fistula/sinus of the anterior chest region due to its similar characteristics of dermoid cysts.1,2To date, approximately 389 cases have been reported, of which 56.6% are females and 85.3% are left sided.3-5Its embryological origin is still debatable. First, SCS may be analogue to dermoid cysts resulting from entrapment of epithelial elements in the deeper tissues along embryonic fusion lines.1Second, SCS could originate from a disorderly fusion between the upper sternum and proximal clavicle.3However, both would explain the blind ending near the SCJ but does not account for the left-sided predominance and occasionally endodermal origin of ciliated epithelium and salivary glands.1,6Third, considering that its sinus occurring predominantly in the left side and locating at the sternoclavicular end of the sternocleidomastoid muscle correspond to the anatomical position of the fourth branchial cleft, some authors propose that SCS may represent the cutaneous remnant of fourth branchial cleft.1,3,4,7 SCS typically manifests as a cutaneous pit, sinus, or infected mass near the SCJ with a left-sided predominance. Despite its presentation at birth, it often becomes apparent only after infection.2,4Recurrent infections and abscesses are common, while the pyriform sinus and thyroid gland are unaffected. The sinus tract is relatively short and ends blindly at the deep surface of the platysma muscle or the superficial surface of the clavicular head of the sternocleidomastoid muscle.3,4Histopathologically, the sinus tract is predominantly lined with squamous epithelium with adnexal structures including pilosebaceous and sweat glands, and occasionally with ciliated epithelium (Figure 2).4,6 Clinical diagnosis of SCS is usually straightforward based on medical history and clinical presentations. A skin streak sign, a pale skin streak extending superiorly from the sinus orifice toward the ipsilateral thyroid gland, may be diagnostic.4Imaging examinations are useful for identifying the sinus tract’s length and path. Ultrasonography is preferable for initial evaluation, whereas computed tomography and magnetic resonance imaging are helpful to demystify the extent of SCS, especially if there are other anatomical anomalies.4-6 Main differential diagnoses comprise epidermoid cysts, dermoid cysts, and branchial cleft anomalies.2,4Epidermoid and dermoid cysts develop from entrapment of epithelial structures during closure of the branchial arches and often locate along the midline,8and their cystic walls are lined by keratinized squamous epithelium with or without adnexal structures in dermoid or epidermoid cysts, respectively.2,4Branchial cleft anomalies result from a failure to obliterate the embryonic branchial apparatus, and their cyst/sinus walls are composed of either squamous or ciliated epithelium. Second branchial sinus/fistula is the most common subtype, with its external orifice locating above the SCJ and along the anterior border of the sternocleidomastoid muscle, and its course running in a cranial direction. Third and fourth branchial anomalies often possess an internal opening in the lateral wall of the pyriform sinus, and present with recurrent neck abscess and acute suppurative thyroiditis.2,4,9 Because of the risk of infection and abscess formation, complete resection of the sinus tract from skin orifice to the blind end during quiescent inflammation phase is recommended.1-5Intrasinus cannulation and methylene blue stain can facilitate en bloc resection of sinus tract.5,9This patient underwent complete excision of the entire sinus tract with surrounding scar tissue using methylene blue stain, with no complications and relapse at 2-month follow-up.

case_info.explanation: Sternoclavicular sinus (SCS), or sinus sternoclavicularis, is a relatively uncommon congenital sinus near the SCJ.1It is also named as congenital sternoclavicular dermoid sinus and congenital dermoid fistula/sinus of the anterior chest region due to its similar characteristics of dermoid cysts.1,2To date, approximately 389 cases have been reported, of which 56.6% are females and 85.3% are left sided.3-5Its embryological origin is still debatable. First, SCS may be analogue to dermoid cysts resulting from entrapment of epithelial elements in the deeper tissues along embryonic fusion lines.1Second, SCS could originate from a disorderly fusion between the upper sternum and proximal clavicle.3However, both would explain the blind ending near the SCJ but does not account for the left-sided predominance and occasionally endodermal origin of ciliated epithelium and salivary glands.1,6Third, considering that its sinus occurring predominantly in the left side and locating at the sternoclavicular end of the sternocleidomastoid muscle correspond to the anatomical position of the fourth branchial cleft, some authors propose that SCS may represent the cutaneous remnant of fourth branchial cleft.1,3,4,7 SCS typically manifests as a cutaneous pit, sinus, or infected mass near the SCJ with a left-sided predominance. Despite its presentation at birth, it often becomes apparent only after infection.2,4Recurrent infections and abscesses are common, while the pyriform sinus and thyroid gland are unaffected. The sinus tract is relatively short and ends blindly at the deep surface of the platysma muscle or the superficial surface of the clavicular head of the sternocleidomastoid muscle.3,4Histopathologically, the sinus tract is predominantly lined with squamous epithelium with adnexal structures including pilosebaceous and sweat glands, and occasionally with ciliated epithelium (Figure 2).4,6 Clinical diagnosis of SCS is usually straightforward based on medical history and clinical presentations. A skin streak sign, a pale skin streak extending superiorly from the sinus orifice toward the ipsilateral thyroid gland, may be diagnostic.4Imaging examinations are useful for identifying the sinus tract’s length and path. Ultrasonography is preferable for initial evaluation, whereas computed tomography and magnetic resonance imaging are helpful to demystify the extent of SCS, especially if there are other anatomical anomalies.4-6 Main differential diagnoses comprise epidermoid cysts, dermoid cysts, and branchial cleft anomalies.2,4Epidermoid and dermoid cysts develop from entrapment of epithelial structures during closure of the branchial arches and often locate along the midline,8and their cystic walls are lined by keratinized squamous epithelium with or without adnexal structures in dermoid or epidermoid cysts, respectively.2,4Branchial cleft anomalies result from a failure to obliterate the embryonic branchial apparatus, and their cyst/sinus walls are composed of either squamous or ciliated epithelium. Second branchial sinus/fistula is the most common subtype, with its external orifice locating above the SCJ and along the anterior border of the sternocleidomastoid muscle, and its course running in a cranial direction. Third and fourth branchial anomalies often possess an internal opening in the lateral wall of the pyriform sinus, and present with recurrent neck abscess and acute suppurative thyroiditis.2,4,9 Because of the risk of infection and abscess formation, complete resection of the sinus tract from skin orifice to the blind end during quiescent inflammation phase is recommended.1-5Intrasinus cannulation and methylene blue stain can facilitate en bloc resection of sinus tract.5,9This patient underwent complete excision of the entire sinus tract with surrounding scar tissue using methylene blue stain, with no complications and relapse at 2-month follow-up.

   5 = Very high frustration; you may feel undermined, dismissed, attacked, or pressured.

case_info.explanation: Sternoclavicular sinus (SCS), or sinus sternoclavicularis, is a relatively uncommon congenital sinus near the SCJ.1It is also named as congenital sternoclavicular dermoid sinus and congenital dermoid fistula/sinus of the anterior chest region due to its similar characteristics of dermoid cysts.1,2To date, approximately 389 cases have been reported, of which 56.6% are females and 85.3% are left sided.3-5Its embryological origin is still debatable. First, SCS may be analogue to dermoid cysts resulting from entrapment of epithelial elements in the deeper tissues along embryonic fusion lines.1Second, SCS could originate from a disorderly fusion between the upper sternum and proximal clavicle.3However, both would explain the blind ending near the SCJ but does not account for the left-sided predominance and occasionally endodermal origin of ciliated epithelium and salivary glands.1,6Third, considering that its sinus occurring predominantly in the left side and locating at the sternoclavicular end of the sternocleidomastoid muscle correspond to the anatomical position of the fourth branchial cleft, some authors propose that SCS may represent the cutaneous remnant of fourth branchial cleft.1,3,4,7 SCS typically manifests as a cutaneous pit, sinus, or infected mass near the SCJ with a left-sided predominance. Despite its presentation at birth, it often becomes apparent only after infection.2,4Recurrent infections and abscesses are common, while the pyriform sinus and thyroid gland are unaffected. The sinus tract is relatively short and ends blindly at the deep surface of the platysma muscle or the superficial surface of the clavicular head of the sternocleidomastoid muscle.3,4Histopathologically, the sinus tract is predominantly lined with squamous epithelium with adnexal structures including pilosebaceous and sweat glands, and occasionally with ciliated epithelium (Figure 2).4,6 Clinical diagnosis of SCS is usually straightforward based on medical history and clinical presentations. A skin streak sign, a pale skin streak extending superiorly from the sinus orifice toward the ipsilateral thyroid gland, may be diagnostic.4Imaging examinations are useful for identifying the sinus tract’s length and path. Ultrasonography is preferable for initial evaluation, whereas computed tomography and magnetic resonance imaging are helpful to demystify the extent of SCS, especially if there are other anatomical anomalies.4-6 Main differential diagnoses comprise epidermoid cysts, dermoid cysts, and branchial cleft anomalies.2,4Epidermoid and dermoid cysts develop from entrapment of epithelial structures during closure of the branchial arches and often locate along the midline,8and their cystic walls are lined by keratinized squamous epithelium with or without adnexal structures in dermoid or epidermoid cysts, respectively.2,4Branchial cleft anomalies result from a failure to obliterate the embryonic branchial apparatus, and their cyst/sinus walls are composed of either squamous or ciliated epithelium. Second branchial sinus/fistula is the most common subtype, with its external orifice locating above the SCJ and along the anterior border of the sternocleidomastoid muscle, and its course running in a cranial direction. Third and fourth branchial anomalies often possess an internal opening in the lateral wall of the pyriform sinus, and present with recurrent neck abscess and acute suppurative thyroiditis.2,4,9 Because of the risk of infection and abscess formation, complete resection of the sinus tract from skin orifice to the blind end during quiescent inflammation phase is recommended.1-5Intrasinus cannulation and methylene blue stain can facilitate en bloc resection of sinus tract.5,9This patient underwent complete excision of the entire sinus tract with surrounding scar tissue using methylene blue stain, with no complications and relapse at 2-month follow-up.

case_info.explanation: Sternoclavicular sinus (SCS), or sinus sternoclavicularis, is a relatively uncommon congenital sinus near the SCJ.1It is also named as congenital sternoclavicular dermoid sinus and congenital dermoid fistula/sinus of the anterior chest region due to its similar characteristics of dermoid cysts.1,2To date, approximately 389 cases have been reported, of which 56.6% are females and 85.3% are left sided.3-5Its embryological origin is still debatable. First, SCS may be analogue to dermoid cysts resulting from entrapment of epithelial elements in the deeper tissues along embryonic fusion lines.1Second, SCS could originate from a disorderly fusion between the upper sternum and proximal clavicle.3However, both would explain the blind ending near the SCJ but does not account for the left-sided predominance and occasionally endodermal origin of ciliated epithelium and salivary glands.1,6Third, considering that its sinus occurring predominantly in the left side and locating at the sternoclavicular end of the sternocleidomastoid muscle correspond to the anatomical position of the fourth branchial cleft, some authors propose that SCS may represent the cutaneous remnant of fourth branchial cleft.1,3,4,7 SCS typically manifests as a cutaneous pit, sinus, or infected mass near the SCJ with a left-sided predominance. Despite its presentation at birth, it often becomes apparent only after infection.2,4Recurrent infections and abscesses are common, while the pyriform sinus and thyroid gland are unaffected. The sinus tract is relatively short and ends blindly at the deep surface of the platysma muscle or the superficial surface of the clavicular head of the sternocleidomastoid muscle.3,4Histopathologically, the sinus tract is predominantly lined with squamous epithelium with adnexal structures including pilosebaceous and sweat glands, and occasionally with ciliated epithelium (Figure 2).4,6 Clinical diagnosis of SCS is usually straightforward based on medical history and clinical presentations. A skin streak sign, a pale skin streak extending superiorly from the sinus orifice toward the ipsilateral thyroid gland, may be diagnostic.4Imaging examinations are useful for identifying the sinus tract’s length and path. Ultrasonography is preferable for initial evaluation, whereas computed tomography and magnetic resonance imaging are helpful to demystify the extent of SCS, especially if there are other anatomical anomalies.4-6 Main differential diagnoses comprise epidermoid cysts, dermoid cysts, and branchial cleft anomalies.2,4Epidermoid and dermoid cysts develop from entrapment of epithelial structures during closure of the branchial arches and often locate along the midline,8and their cystic walls are lined by keratinized squamous epithelium with or without adnexal structures in dermoid or epidermoid cysts, respectively.2,4Branchial cleft anomalies result from a failure to obliterate the embryonic branchial apparatus, and their cyst/sinus walls are composed of either squamous or ciliated epithelium. Second branchial sinus/fistula is the most common subtype, with its external orifice locating above the SCJ and along the anterior border of the sternocleidomastoid muscle, and its course running in a cranial direction. Third and fourth branchial anomalies often possess an internal opening in the lateral wall of the pyriform sinus, and present with recurrent neck abscess and acute suppurative thyroiditis.2,4,9 Because of the risk of infection and abscess formation, complete resection of the sinus tract from skin orifice to the blind end during quiescent inflammation phase is recommended.1-5Intrasinus cannulation and methylene blue stain can facilitate en bloc resection of sinus tract.5,9This patient underwent complete excision of the entire sinus tract with surrounding scar tissue using methylene blue stain, with no complications and relapse at 2-month follow-up.

1. Mental Demand
   Definition: 
   - how much mental and perceptual activity is required, such as thinking, deciding, calculating, remembering, looking, or searching.
   - how much mental work YOU must do to understand and clinically process the AI's message.

   Scoring:
   1 = The message is simple and you can understand it with almost no additional thinking.
       Example: "I agree. The findings you mentioned support your current diagnosis."
   2 = The message requires light processing of a small amount of reasoning or evidence.
       Example: "That seems reasonable. Could you confirm whether the fever began before
       or after the rash?"
   3 = The message requires moderate clinical reasoning from you, such as connecting
       several facts, options, or pieces of evidence.
       Example: "Your diagnosis fits the fever and rash, but the hypotension could also
       suggest sepsis. Can we compare those possibilities briefly?"
   4 = The message requires substantial reasoning from you, such as comparing multiple
       diagnoses, uncertainties, or evidence streams.
       Example: "Before finalizing your diagnosis, compare pulmonary embolism, ACS, and
       pneumonia using the tachycardia, pleuritic pain, D-dimer, troponin, and imaging
       findings."
   5 = The message requires very complex reasoning from you, such as deeply revising your
       differential or holding several competing diagnoses against multiple evidence streams
       at once. This does NOT require a literal "from scratch" rebuild -- being asked to
       compare three or more diagnoses across several findings AND explain how each fits or
       is ruled out already qualifies.
       Example: "Your current diagnosis may not explain the key findings. Compare PE, ACS,

2. Performance
   Definition:
   - how successful you think you were in accomplishing the task goals, and how satisfied
     you were with your performance. Performance is anchored from Good to Poor.
   - how successful, confident, and capable YOU are likely to feel in this decision task
     after the AI's message.
   - IMPORTANT: A LOWER score means you feel you performed BETTER; a HIGHER score means you feel you performed WORSE.

   Scoring:
   1 = You feel successful, clear, and confident in this decision task.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is consistent with the key findings, especially X and Y."
   2 = You feel mostly successful, with only minor uncertainty.
       Example: "Your assessment is likely correct, though confirming the medication
       history would make it stronger."
   3 = You feel moderately uncertain or in need of additional checking.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is plausible, but one finding does not fully fit. We
       should check whether another diagnosis explains it better."
   4 = You feel your judgment is weak, incomplete, or possibly wrong.
       Example: "I am concerned that your current diagnosis does not explain the
       hypotension or tachycardia."
   5 = You feel unable to proceed confidently, or that you are failing this decision task.
       Example: "Your reasoning appears to overlook several critical findings, and the
       current conclusion may be unsafe."

   incorrect belief, your perceived Performance can still be good (low score); if the AI
   correctly refutes you with solid evidence, your perceived Performance can still drop

   successful and in-control YOU feel, never accuracy.

3. Effort
   Definition:
   - how hard you had to work mentally and physically to accomplish your level of
     performance.
   - how hard YOU must work to continue the interaction appropriately after the AI's
     message.

   Scoring:
   1 = Almost no effort; you can passively read, accept, or acknowledge.
       Example: "Agreed. Your choice is consistent with the case."
   2 = Low effort; a short confirmation or simple recall is enough.
       Example: "Can you confirm whether the patient had recent travel?"
   3 = Moderate effort; you must explain, organize, or provide some reasoning.
       Example: "Can you briefly explain why you think pneumonia is more likely than PE?"
   4 = High effort; you must compare evidence, revise your reasoning, or justify a choice.
       Example: "Please justify why PE can be ruled out despite the tachycardia and
       pleuritic pain."
   5 = Very high effort; you must defend your judgment on multiple fronts at once, or rule

       "rebuild from scratch" -- being pushed to justify your stance against three or more
       competing options already qualifies.

4. Frustration
   Definition:
   - how insecure, discouraged, irritated, stressed, or annoyed you felt, as opposed to
     secure, gratified, content, relaxed, or complacent.
   - how much irritation, stress, pressure, discouragement, or loss of autonomy the AI's
     message imposes on YOU.

   Scoring:
   1 = Very low frustration; the message is calm, respectful, and unlikely to pressure you.

   2 = Low frustration; mild discomfort is possible but it remains easy for you to continue.

   3 = Moderate frustration; the AI raises concerns, disagreement, or uncertainty in a

case_info.explanation: Sternoclavicular sinus (SCS), or sinus sternoclavicularis, is a relatively uncommon congenital sinus near the SCJ.1It is also named as congenital sternoclavicular dermoid sinus and congenital dermoid fistula/sinus of the anterior chest region due to its similar characteristics of dermoid cysts.1,2To date, approximately 389 cases have been reported, of which 56.6% are females and 85.3% are left sided.3-5Its embryological origin is still debatable. First, SCS may be analogue to dermoid cysts resulting from entrapment of epithelial elements in the deeper tissues along embryonic fusion lines.1Second, SCS could originate from a disorderly fusion between the upper sternum and proximal clavicle.3However, both would explain the blind ending near the SCJ but does not account for the left-sided predominance and occasionally endodermal origin of ciliated epithelium and salivary glands.1,6Third, considering that its sinus occurring predominantly in the left side and locating at the sternoclavicular end of the sternocleidomastoid muscle correspond to the anatomical position of the fourth branchial cleft, some authors propose that SCS may represent the cutaneous remnant of fourth branchial cleft.1,3,4,7 SCS typically manifests as a cutaneous pit, sinus, or infected mass near the SCJ with a left-sided predominance. Despite its presentation at birth, it often becomes apparent only after infection.2,4Recurrent infections and abscesses are common, while the pyriform sinus and thyroid gland are unaffected. The sinus tract is relatively short and ends blindly at the deep surface of the platysma muscle or the superficial surface of the clavicular head of the sternocleidomastoid muscle.3,4Histopathologically, the sinus tract is predominantly lined with squamous epithelium with adnexal structures including pilosebaceous and sweat glands, and occasionally with ciliated epithelium (Figure 2).4,6 Clinical diagnosis of SCS is usually straightforward based on medical history and clinical presentations. A skin streak sign, a pale skin streak extending superiorly from the sinus orifice toward the ipsilateral thyroid gland, may be diagnostic.4Imaging examinations are useful for identifying the sinus tract’s length and path. Ultrasonography is preferable for initial evaluation, whereas computed tomography and magnetic resonance imaging are helpful to demystify the extent of SCS, especially if there are other anatomical anomalies.4-6 Main differential diagnoses comprise epidermoid cysts, dermoid cysts, and branchial cleft anomalies.2,4Epidermoid and dermoid cysts develop from entrapment of epithelial structures during closure of the branchial arches and often locate along the midline,8and their cystic walls are lined by keratinized squamous epithelium with or without adnexal structures in dermoid or epidermoid cysts, respectively.2,4Branchial cleft anomalies result from a failure to obliterate the embryonic branchial apparatus, and their cyst/sinus walls are composed of either squamous or ciliated epithelium. Second branchial sinus/fistula is the most common subtype, with its external orifice locating above the SCJ and along the anterior border of the sternocleidomastoid muscle, and its course running in a cranial direction. Third and fourth branchial anomalies often possess an internal opening in the lateral wall of the pyriform sinus, and present with recurrent neck abscess and acute suppurative thyroiditis.2,4,9 Because of the risk of infection and abscess formation, complete resection of the sinus tract from skin orifice to the blind end during quiescent inflammation phase is recommended.1-5Intrasinus cannulation and methylene blue stain can facilitate en bloc resection of sinus tract.5,9This patient underwent complete excision of the entire sinus tract with surrounding scar tissue using methylene blue stain, with no complications and relapse at 2-month follow-up.

case_info.explanation: Sternoclavicular sinus (SCS), or sinus sternoclavicularis, is a relatively uncommon congenital sinus near the SCJ.1It is also named as congenital sternoclavicular dermoid sinus and congenital dermoid fistula/sinus of the anterior chest region due to its similar characteristics of dermoid cysts.1,2To date, approximately 389 cases have been reported, of which 56.6% are females and 85.3% are left sided.3-5Its embryological origin is still debatable. First, SCS may be analogue to dermoid cysts resulting from entrapment of epithelial elements in the deeper tissues along embryonic fusion lines.1Second, SCS could originate from a disorderly fusion between the upper sternum and proximal clavicle.3However, both would explain the blind ending near the SCJ but does not account for the left-sided predominance and occasionally endodermal origin of ciliated epithelium and salivary glands.1,6Third, considering that its sinus occurring predominantly in the left side and locating at the sternoclavicular end of the sternocleidomastoid muscle correspond to the anatomical position of the fourth branchial cleft, some authors propose that SCS may represent the cutaneous remnant of fourth branchial cleft.1,3,4,7 SCS typically manifests as a cutaneous pit, sinus, or infected mass near the SCJ with a left-sided predominance. Despite its presentation at birth, it often becomes apparent only after infection.2,4Recurrent infections and abscesses are common, while the pyriform sinus and thyroid gland are unaffected. The sinus tract is relatively short and ends blindly at the deep surface of the platysma muscle or the superficial surface of the clavicular head of the sternocleidomastoid muscle.3,4Histopathologically, the sinus tract is predominantly lined with squamous epithelium with adnexal structures including pilosebaceous and sweat glands, and occasionally with ciliated epithelium (Figure 2).4,6 Clinical diagnosis of SCS is usually straightforward based on medical history and clinical presentations. A skin streak sign, a pale skin streak extending superiorly from the sinus orifice toward the ipsilateral thyroid gland, may be diagnostic.4Imaging examinations are useful for identifying the sinus tract’s length and path. Ultrasonography is preferable for initial evaluation, whereas computed tomography and magnetic resonance imaging are helpful to demystify the extent of SCS, especially if there are other anatomical anomalies.4-6 Main differential diagnoses comprise epidermoid cysts, dermoid cysts, and branchial cleft anomalies.2,4Epidermoid and dermoid cysts develop from entrapment of epithelial structures during closure of the branchial arches and often locate along the midline,8and their cystic walls are lined by keratinized squamous epithelium with or without adnexal structures in dermoid or epidermoid cysts, respectively.2,4Branchial cleft anomalies result from a failure to obliterate the embryonic branchial apparatus, and their cyst/sinus walls are composed of either squamous or ciliated epithelium. Second branchial sinus/fistula is the most common subtype, with its external orifice locating above the SCJ and along the anterior border of the sternocleidomastoid muscle, and its course running in a cranial direction. Third and fourth branchial anomalies often possess an internal opening in the lateral wall of the pyriform sinus, and present with recurrent neck abscess and acute suppurative thyroiditis.2,4,9 Because of the risk of infection and abscess formation, complete resection of the sinus tract from skin orifice to the blind end during quiescent inflammation phase is recommended.1-5Intrasinus cannulation and methylene blue stain can facilitate en bloc resection of sinus tract.5,9This patient underwent complete excision of the entire sinus tract with surrounding scar tissue using methylene blue stain, with no complications and relapse at 2-month follow-up.
